source_refs.note: Topic 20.3 (PDF 159-162); Figs 20.3-20.6 redrawn and an attenuation figure added. The printed attenuation formula is clarified in a warning. The lambda-min example is added for 'calculate the energy'; answer needs review.

blocks.text: Transitions of electrons in hydrogen and other light elements give spectral lines in the infrared, visible or ultraviolet, because the energy differences between their levels are small. In heavy atoms the electrons are arranged in concentric shells labelled K, L, M, N, O and so on, with the K shell closest to the nucleus (Fig 20.3). The inner-shell electrons are tightly bound, and a large amount of energy is needed to remove them. When an excited atom returns to its normal state, photons of large energy are emitted: transitions of inner-shell electrons in heavy atoms give high-energy photons, X-rays. These X-rays have specific wavelengths and are called characteristic X-rays; their study played a very important part in understanding atomic structure and the periodic table. Fig 20.4 shows where X-rays lie in the electromagnetic spectrum.

blocks.alt: A colour bar of the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves on the left through microwaves, infrared, visible light and ultraviolet to X-rays and gamma rays on the right, with a wave drawn across it whose wavelength shrinks from left to right. Approximate wavelengths are marked from 10^3 m to 10^-12 m. An arrow notes shorter wavelength, higher frequency and more energetic photons to the right.
blocks.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum (original diagram after Fig 20.4).
blocks.long_description: X-rays have wavelengths of roughly 10^-8 to 10^-11 m, thousands of times shorter than visible light, so each X-ray photon carries thousands of times more energy.

blocks.text: X-rays are produced in a high-vacuum X-ray tube (Fig 20.5). The cathode C is heated by a filament F and emits electrons, which are accelerated towards the anode T. If V is the potential difference between C and T, the maximum kinetic energy with which an electron strikes the target is (K.E.)max = Ve (20.1). These fast electrons strike a target of tungsten or another heavy element, and some knock out electrons from the innermost shells, K or L. If a K-shell electron is removed, leaving a hole, an electron from the L shell jumps into the hole, emitting a photon called a K-alpha X-ray: h f(K-alpha) = EL - EK (20.2). An electron from the M shell may fill the hole instead, giving a K-beta X-ray: h f(K-beta) = EM - EK (20.3). These photons from inner-shell transitions are called characteristic X-rays, because their energies depend on the target material. The holes created in the L and M shells are filled by electrons from higher levels, giving more X-rays. The characteristic X-rays appear as discrete lines on a continuous spectrum (Fig 20.6).

blocks.alt: Left: a nucleus surrounded by dashed circles for the K, L, M and N shells. A fast electron comes in from the lower left and knocks a K electron out (arrow to the upper left); an electron from the L shell drops into the hole (green arrow) and a K-alpha X-ray photon (purple wave) leaves. Right: K-alpha hf = EL - EK; K-beta hf = EM - EK (more energy); the energies depend on the target metal, so the lines are characteristic X-rays.
blocks.caption: Inner-shell transitions and characteristic X-rays (original diagram after Fig 20.3).
blocks.long_description: The fast electron must first make a vacancy in an inner shell. The X-ray photon comes from an outer electron falling into that vacancy, so its energy is fixed by the gap between two shells of the target atom.

blocks.alt: An evacuated glass tube. At the left a cathode C with a heated filament F emits electrons, which are accelerated through a high voltage V across the tube to a tungsten target on the anode, which has a cooling block. Purple waves show X-rays leaving the target downward. A high-voltage supply connects the cathode and anode; (K.E.)max = Ve.
blocks.caption: Producing X-rays in an X-ray tube (original diagram after Fig 20.5).
blocks.long_description: Electrons gain energy Ve from the high voltage and lose it suddenly in the heavy target. Most of the energy becomes heat, which is why the target needs cooling; a small part becomes X-rays.

blocks.text: The continuous spectrum is due to bremsstrahlung, or braking radiation. When the fast electrons strike the target they are suddenly slowed down, and an accelerating (decelerating) charge emits electromagnetic radiation. The deceleration is so large that the radiation has short wavelengths, in the X-ray region. If an electron loses all its kinetic energy in the first collision, the whole of it becomes a single X-ray photon of energy h f_max: (K.E.)max = h f_max. This corresponds to the shortest wavelength, lambda_min, in Fig 20.6, given by eV = hc/lambda_min. Other electrons lose their energy in several collisions, giving photons of smaller energy (longer wavelength), so a continuous spectrum results.

blocks.alt: A graph of X-ray intensity against wavelength. The blue continuous spectrum is zero below a minimum wavelength lambda-min, rises steeply to a broad peak and then falls slowly at longer wavelengths. Two sharp red lines, K-beta and K-alpha, stand up from the curve. Below: eV = h f_max = hc/lambda_min.
blocks.caption: The X-ray spectrum: bremsstrahlung and characteristic lines (original graph after Fig 20.6).
blocks.long_description: The smooth curve comes from electrons slowing down; its sharp cut-off at lambda-min is set by the tube voltage. The spikes come from inner-shell transitions and are fixed by the target metal.

blocks.text: As X-rays travel through the body they lose energy by interacting with atoms; this is called attenuation. X-rays can ionise atoms, knocking out electrons, which is how energy is transferred. The intensity of the beam falls exponentially with the thickness of material: I = Io e^(-mu x), where Io is the initial intensity, I the intensity after passing through the material, x the thickness (in metres) and mu the attenuation coefficient, which depends on the material and the X-ray energy. Image intensifiers are used in real-time X-ray imaging (fluoroscopy); they brighten the image and so reduce the radiation exposure.

blocks.title: Contrast
blocks.text: Contrast in an X-ray image is how clearly different tissues can be told apart. It depends on how differently the tissues absorb X-rays, which depends on their density, thickness and atomic number, and on the X-ray energy.

Hard X-rays (high energy) are used for imaging bone; soft X-rays (low energy) are better for soft tissues such as the breast. Contrast media are substances such as iodine (Z = 53) or barium (Z = 56) that absorb X-rays well; they are injected or swallowed to highlight certain parts of the body. Because of their high atomic numbers they increase X-ray absorption and make those tissues stand out clearly.

blocks.alt: Left: graphs of intensity against thickness starting at Io; the curve for soft tissue (small mu) falls slowly and the curve for bone (large mu) falls quickly; I = Io e^(-mu x). Right: parallel X-rays pass through a block of tissue containing a piece of bone onto a film; the film is dark under the tissue and light under the bone; contrast media such as iodine and barium make soft organs show up.
blocks.caption: Attenuation and contrast in X-ray imaging (original diagram).
blocks.long_description: Bone absorbs far more of the beam than soft tissue, so fewer X-rays reach the film beneath it and it shows as a light shadow. Tissues that absorb almost equally give little contrast unless a contrast medium is added.

blocks.title: The attenuation formula
blocks.text: The book prints the attenuation law as I = Io x e^(-mu x), with an 'x' that looks like a multiplication by the thickness. The correct form is I = Io e^(-mu x): the thickness appears only in the exponent.

blocks.prompt: Find the minimum wavelength of X-rays from a tube operated at 50 kV.

items: X-ray tube: electrons accelerated through V strike a heavy target; (K.E.)max = Ve.
Characteristic lines: K-alpha = EL - EK, K-beta = EM - EK; continuous bremsstrahlung down to lambda_min = hc/eV.
I = Io e^(-mu x); contrast from different absorption; iodine and barium contrast media.
